etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English laughen, laghen, from (Anglian) Old English hlæhhan, hlehhan, (West Saxon) hliehhan, from Proto-West Germanic *hlahhjan, from Proto-Germanic *hlahjaną.

definitions.definition: An expression of mirth particular to the human species; the sound heard in laughing; laughter.

quote.citation: 1803, Oliver Goldsmith, The Poetical Works of Oliver Goldsmith, M.B.: With an Account of His Life, page 45:
quote.text: And the loud laugh that spoke the vacant mind.

quote.citation: 1869, F. W. Robertson, Lectures and Addresses on Literary and Social Topics, page 87:
quote.text: That man is a bad man who has not within him the power of a hearty laugh.

definitions.definition: Something that provokes mirth or scorn.

quote.citation: 1921, Ring Lardner, The Big Town: How I and the Mrs. Go to New York to See Life and Get Katie a Husband, The Bobbs-Merrill Company, page 73:
quote.text: “And this rug,” he says, stomping on an old rag carpet. “How much do you suppose that cost?” ¶ It was my first guess, so I said fifty dollars. ¶ “That’s a laugh,” he said. “I paid two thousand for that rug.”

quote.citation: 1979, Monty Python, Always Look on the Bright Side of Life:
quote.text: Life's a piece of shit / When you look at it / Life's a laugh and death's a joke, it's true.

quote.citation: 2010, The Times, March 14, 2010, Tamzin Outhwaite, the unlikely musical star
quote.text: Outhwaite is a good laugh, yes, she knows how to smile: but deep down, she really is strong and stern.

definitions.definition: (intransitive) To show mirth, satisfaction, or derision, by peculiar movement of the muscles of the face, particularly of the mouth, causing a lighting up of the face and eyes, and usually accompanied by the emission of explosive or chuckling sounds from the chest and throat; to indulge in laughter.

quote.citation: c. 1602 (date written), William Shakespeare, The Famous Historie of Troylus and Cresseid. […] (First Quarto), London:  […]  G[eorge] Eld for R[ichard] Bonian and H[enry] Walley, […], published 1609, →OCLC, [Act I, scene ii]:
quote.text: But there was ſuch laughing, Queen Hecuba laught that her eyes ran ore.

quote.citation: 1807, William Wordsworth, “[I Wandered Lonely as a Cloud]”, in Poems, in Two Volumes, volume II, London:  […]  Longman, Hurst, Rees, and Orme, […], →OCLC, stanza 2, page 49:
quote.text: The waves beside them danced, but they / Outdid the sparkling waves in glee:— / A Poet could not but be gay / In such a laughing company:  […]

The roars of laughter which greeted his proclamation were of two qualities; some men laughing because they knew all about cuckoo-clocks, and other men laughing because they had concluded that the eccentric Jake had been victimised by some wise child of civilisation.

quote.citation: 1979, Monty Python, Always Look on the Bright Side of Life:
quote.text: If life seems jolly rotten / There's something you've forgotten / And that's to laugh and smile and dance and sing.

definitions.definition: (intransitive, figuratively, obsolete) To be or appear cheerful, pleasant, mirthful, lively, or brilliant; to sparkle; to sport.

quote.citation: a. 1701 (date written), John Dryden, “Of the Pythagorean Philosophy. From the Fifteenth Book of Ovid’s Metamorphoses”, in The Miscellaneous Works of John Dryden, […], volume IV, London:  […]  J[acob] and R[ichard] Tonson, […], published 1760, →OCLC, page 51:
quote.text: The green ſtem grows in ſtature and in ſize, / But only feeds with hope the farmer's eyes; / Then laughs the childiſh year with flow'rets crowned, / And laviſhly prefumes the fields around, / But no ſubſtantial nouriſhment receives, / Infirm the ſtalks, unſolid are the leaves.

quote.citation: 1733, [Alexander Pope], An Essay on Man. […], epistle II, London: Printed for J[ohn] Wilford, […], →OCLC, page 17:
quote.text: In Folly’s Cup ſtill laughs the Bubble, Joy; [...]

definitions.definition: (intransitive, followed by "at") To make an object of laughter or ridicule; to make fun of; to deride; to mock.

quote.citation: 1735, Alexander Pope, “Epistle III. To Allen Lord Bathurst.”, in The Works of Mr. Alexander Pope, volume II, London:  […]  J. Wright, for Lawton Gilliver […], →OCLC, page 23, lines 311–314:
quote.text: No Wit to flatter, left of all his ſtore! / No Fool to laugh at, which he valued more. / There, victor of his health, of fortune, friends, / And fame, this lord of uſeleſs, thouſands ends.

quote.citation: 1891, Oscar Wilde, chapter IV, in The Picture of Dorian Gray, London, New York, N.Y., Melbourne, Vic.: Ward Lock & Co., →OCLC, page 71:
quote.text: There was something about him, Harry, that amused me. He was such a monster. You will laugh at me, I know, but I really went in and paid a whole guinea for the stage-box. To the present day I can't make out why I did so; [...]
On the corner is a banker with a motorcar / The little children laugh at him behind his back

definitions.definition: (transitive) To affect or influence by means of laughter or ridicule.

quote.citation: 1610–1611 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Tempest”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act II, scene i], page 7, column 2:
quote.text: Will you laugh me aſleepe, for I am very heauy.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To express by, or utter with, laughter.

quote.citation: c. 1602 (date written), William Shakespeare, The Famous Historie of Troylus and Cresseid. […] (First Quarto), London:  […]  G[eorge] Eld for R[ichard] Bonian and H[enry] Walley, […], published 1609, →OCLC, [Act I, scene iii]:
quote.text: From his deepe cheſt laughes out a lowd applauſe, [...]

quote.citation: 1866, Louisa May Alcott, chapter 8, in Behind a Mask, or A Woman’s Power:
quote.text: Fairfax addressed her as "my lady," she laughed her musical laugh, and glanced up at a picture of Gerald with eyes full of exultation.
"You refuse to take me seriously," Lute said, when she had laughed her appreciation. "How can I take that Planchette rigmarole seriously?"
